en: Preface to the *Xiudingke Xu*:
In the past, several hundred years after the Buddha-dharma had entered China, Dharma Master Huiyuan finally gathered the multitude of spirits together through the Pure Land.
Although one hundred and twenty-three people were unable to complete their task within a single lifetime, nevertheless—
There were not a few who attained liberation while still alive. These one hundred and twenty-three individuals all bound themselves together through their great vows;
they deeply harmonized with the Buddha’s aspiration, fully manifested the fragrance of the lotus, and successively delivered both enemies and kin, leading their relatives and associates to rebirth.

Subsequently, there were those who awakened to mindfulness of the Buddha upon hearing the sound of water, those who entered into tranquil samādhi to depart for the Western Pure Land, and those whose dreams and divine omens shone with radiant brilliance.

In China, these are all manifestations of the mutual arising of light and darkness within this single lineage. In the Gate of the Patriarchs (*Zongmen*), awareness is lofty and power penetrates deeply;

they stride high above humans and devas, proceeding directly toward the supreme realm of quiescent light (*anuttara-śānta-prabhā*). They provisionally suppress the three types of pure lands (*sukhāvati*:

*vipāka*, *upāya*, and *sahā*)—which are like sweet fragrances that do not cling—and favor the wondrous and supreme *amṛta*. However, if one does not encounter those of superior faculties, this will inevitably be transformed into poison. Thus, Cao...
Chan Master Yongming, the eighth-generation descendant of Master Xuefeng, returned the full radiance of the *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Source) and entered the single lineage of the Western Land.
Among all the dharma-gates, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is most complete. The Great Master Yunqi, possessing correct knowledge and vision, roamed the dharma-ocean of the *Avataṃsaka*.

With profound compassion and outstanding discernment, his contemplation was refined and his application vast; he composed the *Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*, leading [practitioners] back [to the Pure Land] with meticulous detail.
The Land of Ultimate Bliss. Sincerely reciting the Buddha’s name brings joy to devas and dragons; immeasurable sentient beings find it like obtaining a compassionate mother.

Therefore, among those of both the Chan and Dharma-lecture schools who have not yet attained freedom from future rebirths, there are none who do not regard this as the place where their spiritual spirits find rest.
Among those of both the Chan and Dharma-lecture schools who have already attained freedom from future rebirths, there are none who do not regard this as [their] water.

Regarding the conditions for the Moon Dharma-Assembly: having already attained liberation for oneself, one now delivers others through the peerless Dharma. Beyond this single gate of rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha, what else could there be?
Alas! His spirit roams the Dharma-realm, radiant and crystalline, as he traverses the gardens of the Three Teachings.
My friend Zhengzi has now nearly attained the ultimate destination of single-mindedness.
He has authored forty-eight works in the *Zongjing Tang Congshu*, of which the *Xiuding Ke* (The Ritual for Cultivating Samādhi) is the first. Upon seeing it, I felt a heart of joy;
I consulted with my kinsmen and took the initiative to have it carved for printing. I pray that those throughout the ten directions who possess faith will together receive this radiance.
"Using the Ear. Renhe Xu Yue’s own preface states:
"Without concentration, there is no precept; without concentration, there is no wisdom. One who lacks concentration is a manifestation of saṃsāra.
Among all sentient beings, since beginningless kalpas, who has not performed good deeds? Who has not practiced cultivation? Who has not..."
Regarding the recitation of the Buddha’s name: who has not made the vow? Yet, because the light of the mind is not fixed, one has not been born in the Pure Land;
thus, for a long time, one drifts and sinks, failing to receive liberation. How bitter! How painful!

If you rely upon this book and practice it daily, there will surely come a time when the radiant light comes to welcome and lead you. May those who are kinsmen across three lifetimes exert themselves together. The 11th year of the Xianfeng era.
First Month. Prepared and annotated by the practitioners of Pure Practice, the Bodhisattva Precepts-holders Zheng Chengde (Xuechuan) and Zheng Chengyuan (Xuelang).
We respectfully set forth this account of its origins. By this merit, may our sovereign and father be peaceful and secure;
may their pure practice flourish and their wisdom-voice be fully realized.
First, offer incense and praise:
The heart-incense is now ignited; its fragrance permeates the entire Dharma-realm. All those gathered at the Lotus Pond hear it from afar.
Our Buddha raises auspicious clouds, Amidst a profusion of magnificent omens, To welcome and guide us.
The vow is earnest; auspicious omens swirl in profusion. As the vow to guide others grows ever more earnest, strike the fish-shaped gong once for each circuit.

Faith serves as the incense. Regarding the "Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu): it is defined as the sphere encompassed by all that reaches through both mental phenomena and objective phenomena. Thus it is said.
Its vastness encompasses all things without exception. "The lotus pond assembly" refers to those who dwell in the Pure Land of the West.
"Our Buddha" refers to Amitābha. He is necessarily called "our" because he appears from within the radiance of our own minds;
were that radiance not gathered, one could not perceive the Buddha. As for "arising," it means emerging from the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
They have come to this Sahā world in the eastern land. "Auspicious omens" refers to such things as multi-storied pavilions, banners and streamers, extraordinary fragrances, and celestial music.
"Profuse" means that their patterns and colors intermingle.
"Those whose vows are still earnest" refers to when Amitābha Buddha was practicing his path as the Bhikṣu Dharmākara; before the presence of Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, he made forty-eight [vows].
Through the fulfillment of these eight vows, he shall attain the Way of the Buddha.
These forty-eight vows are all established as manifold skillful means to extensively deliver sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the six realms of existence.

They exhort them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha so that they may be born within the world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), where they shall cultivate their practice without regression, realize the True Dharma, achieve majestic spiritual power, and in turn transform and deliver others.

Now, Amitābha Buddha’s power of vows has been fully realized; he has long since attained Buddhahood. His vow-light shines with compassionate illumination, and his heart of welcoming and guiding is profound.
It is like a single mirror containing the void: when a reflection approaches, it appears. Thus, when one strikes it, there is nothing that does not pass through.
Namo to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Lotus Pond Assembly (three times, with three prostrations).
The Buddha who preached the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is Śākyamuni Buddha of the Sahā world in the eastern direction. Śākyamuni is here in this Sahā world.
He attains Buddhahood. His lifespan corresponds to that of sentient beings, yet it does not exceed a hundred years.

Out of compassion for the beings of this Sahā world—who find it difficult to encounter a Buddha and who will undergo great suffering and affliction for thousands of millions of years between the passing of Śākyamuni and the arrival of Maitreya—he has preached this *Amitābha Sūtra* to circulate throughout the world, so that all suffering beings may practice for seven days.
Through this merit, one is exempted from the sufferings of eternal kalpas; one transforms from the mundane to the sacred and does not regress from the cause of Buddhahood. "Sūtra" means "Dharma.
As for the title *Amitābha*, it exclusively explains the causes, conditions, and meritorious virtues of Amitābha Buddha’s salvation of sentient beings.
"A" means "non-" (or "no"). "Mita" means "measure. Because that Buddha has perfected ten thousand virtues that are inexhaustible, he is called Amitābha.
He is named "Immeasurable. Among the ten thousand virtues, may he be the most supreme. Because his power of aspiration is great, his radiance is immeasurable;
because his aspirational mind is long-lasting, his lifespan is immeasurable. The Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the Buddha of Immeasurable Light mentioned in various sutras are this very Buddha.
Śākyamuni preached this sutra while in the Sahā world, located to the south of the eastern land.
From Jambudvīpa, Śrāvastī, it was transmitted to China; China is the eastern edge of the Southern Continent, where we dwell.
The Sanskrit text is ancient and profound, such that it cannot be recited [as is]. During the Yao Qin period, there was the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva, who translated this sutra.
The meaning of the sutra is perfect and subtle, such that it cannot be fathomed by those of shallow understanding. There is...
Regarding the *Bodhisattva Precepts of the Great Qing Dynasty* by Zheng Xuechuan: this is presented as a "present-day interpretation" (*jinjie*).
This "present-day interpretation" takes the meanings of "presently preaching the Dharma," "presently making vows," and "this present life" from the scriptures;

it hopes that people will achieve their goal within a single lifetime, so as not to enter the womb of a parent again, but instead wondrously grasp the lotus flower and transcend far beyond the realms of existence. ○
The Buddha speaks and I listen; all these arise from the mind. It is simply the mind that speaks and the mind that listens.

The essence of the mind is like a mirror. Mountains, rivers, the great earth, people, things, space, myself, and the Tathāgata—all such diverse forms and categories—are merely reflections manifested within this wondrous, perfect mirror of the mind.
Thus have I heard.
"Thus" (evam) refers to the true essence of the mind, which is like a mirror.

"I" (mayā) refers to the phenomena manifested within the mind, which is like pointing out a single reflection upon that entire mirror. Regarding the term "I," there are two meanings; as stated in the sutra itself: [text continues].
This refers to Ānanda, who compiled the teachings. According to the scriptures, he was one who maintained the recitation.
"Hearing" (wen) is the movement of the wisdom of the mind; it is only when the mind and the ear function together that one may truly be said to hear.
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park (the sound of "Jeta" is *ch'i*).
Regarding "at one time": the temporal divisions of the various devas and humans differ; the Buddha’s voice pervades everywhere and cannot be restricted to a single direction.
"The Buddha" refers to Śākyamuni. He was born during the reign of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty and passed away during the reign of King Mu of the Zhou.
At that time, the King of Great Compassion manifests his shadow to come and deliver sentient beings; he neither dies nor is born, yet he manifests birth and death.
This is like the moon in water, a lamp, or clouds—merely a subtle and wondrous reflection.

The fundamental essence of the Buddha is simply radiance, which swallows and spits out space, reaching everywhere; how could there be coming and going through birth and death? ○ "Buddha" means awakening.
There is no place where he is not awakened, and no time when he is not awakened. Having utterly destroyed all dullness and torpor, he delivers both himself and others;
therefore, he is called a Buddha. In Sanskrit it is called Śrāvastī, which here means "Hearing of Wealth.
Jeta refers to Prince Jeta. Anāthapiṇḍika is the title of the elder. The elder purchased the prince’s grove to provide for the Buddha.
The Crown Prince sold only the grove and did not sell the trees; he personally used the trees to provide for the Buddha. Thus, the grove and the trees are both designated by the name "the Land.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
"Monks (bhikṣu): this term refers to 'alms-seekers' (bhikṣu). Above, they seek the Dharma from the Buddha; below, they seek food from sentient beings.
Saṃgha: this means 'assembly. They are all great Arhats."
The Bodhisattva constitutes the Mahāyāna; the Pratyekabuddha, the Madhyamika-yāna; and the Śrāvaka, the Hīnayāna.
An Arhat is the fourth fruit of the Śrāvaka-yāna. There are three meanings of "Arhat": first, one who can slay the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*);
second, one who terrifies and disperses all Māras; third, one who is worthy of receiving offerings from humans and devas. The Great Arhat...
As for the Arhats: they are those who have resolved their minds on Bodhicitta and subsequently entered the Mahāyāna.
They are well-known to all;
everyone knows their names and recognizes their faces, which signifies that their virtue and reputation are complete. These are one thousand two hundred and five.
There are ten arhats, among whom many shadow-forms of great bodhisattvas appear.
The Elder De-sheng is the leader;

"elder" refers to superior virtue, while "venerable" (lao) refers to seniority in ordination. One year since leaving the household life constitutes one *la* (ordination year). These two terms apply generally.
This refers to the sixteen Arhats mentioned below.
Śāriputra. "Śāri" means "śāli" (crane), and "putra" means "son. The Venerable One’s mother had eyes as clear and bright as a crane.
Śāriputra was thus named the "Son of the Śāri Bird. This Venerable One is foremost in wisdom.
It is said that this single method for aspiring to be reborn [in the Pure Land] cannot be fully believed by those who lack great wisdom; therefore, he is listed at the head.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana: *Mahā* means "great.
*Maudgalyāyana* means "of the clan of Maudgalya" (or "Bean-clan").
Mahākāśyapa (the final syllable "ye" is pronounced "she"):
this is translated as "Great Drinker of Light. Mahākātyāyana.
This is translated as "Greatly Adorned.
Mahākauṣṭhila (the character *chī* is pronounced *xī*) is translated as "Great Thighs."
Revata; this is translated as "Constellation.
Cūḍapanthaka (the final syllable *ka* is pronounced like *gia*).
This is translated as "Succession to the Way.
Nanda is translated as "Virtuous Joy."
Ānanda—here translated as "Joyous Celebration"—was the Buddha’s cousin. He was born on the very day the Buddha attained enlightenment and served as the Buddha’s attendant for several decades.
Much of the Buddha’s canon was compiled by him.
Rāhula means "obscuration" or "covering. When the Buddha was born into the house of King Śuddhodana, he was named Prince Siddhārtha.

When the prince desired to leave the household life, his father the king did not permit it; instead, he had him take a consort so that he might carry on the lineage. Thereupon, the prince pointed with his finger...
The queen’s womb announced: "Six years hence, a son shall be born. After these words were spoken, the Prince immediately renounced the household life.

Because he obstructed his father’s renunciation before dwelling in the mother’s womb, and because he himself obstructed [the prophecy] for six years while dwelling in the womb, it is called "obstructing" (*paticchādeti*).
This Venerable One, having plugged a mouse hole for six days in a previous life, manifested this [result].
Answer:
Gavāmpati (the "Gao" in Gao-fan-bo-ti is pronounced like "jiao").
This means "ox-chewer. After an ox swallows, it regurgitates and chews again; this is called "chewing" (*niṣṭhīvana*). This Venerable One, in a previous life...
Because he reviled others by calling them oxen, he manifested this retribution.
Piṇḍola Bharadvāja: *Piṇḍola* means "Immovable" (*Acala*);
*Bharadvāja* means "Sharp Faculties" (*Tīkṣṇendriya*). This is the name of the Superior.
His clan name was Kālodāyin,
which in this language is translated as "Black Radiance."
Mahākapphiṇa (the *na* and *nu* are pronounced as in "nanuo");
this is translated as "Great Kappa Star. Bakula.
This is translated as "Good Appearance" (Sunetra).
Aniruddha (Aniruddha; *nu* is pronounced as *hou*). This is translated as "Free from Poverty.
This Venerable One was without eyes, yet his mind-eye saw clearly through all things. For this reason, he is placed sixteenth.
This concludes the final section concerning the Western Realm; one should internalize and realize its meaning through the mind and spirit, and thus proceed toward it.
By these sixteen great disciples, one may infer the entire assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty followers.
Together with all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. "Bodhi" (菩) means awakening (*bodhi*);
here it is translated as "awakening. "Sattva" (薩) means *sattva*; here it is translated as "sentient being" (*sattva*).

The upper character encompasses awakening, and the lower character encompasses sentient beings. One who uses the Buddha’s awakening to deliver sentient beings is a bodhisattva. "Mahāsattva" (摩訶薩) likewise...
This refers to sentient beings with the mind of the Great Way.
Mañjuśrī Dharma Prince—Mañjuśrī means "Wondrous Head" (Miaoshou) in this language. This Bodhisattva possesses great wisdom that is unobstructed; [he dwells] in the presence of the Buddha.
It is said: because there is no further doubt, he is listed first. One who possesses mastery over the Dharma is called a "Dharma King," which refers to the Tathāgata.
Great Bodhisattvas are able to transmit the Buddha-Dharma and are thus termed "Princes of the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Ajita.
"Ajita" means "Invincible. This is the name of Maitreya Bodhisattva. "Maitreya" means "Loving-kindness One";
this is the clan name of the Bodhisattva. One million years after Śākyamuni, Maitreya will appear.
Upon attaining Buddhahood, Śākyamuni entrusted all those sentient beings whom he had transformed and liberated but whose capacities were not yet matured to him.

However, among these sentient beings, their spiritual dispositions (*gotra*) are not uniform; some are impatient by nature and cannot endure the cycle of birth and death, being unable to wait for the three assemblies at the Dragon Flower tree after ten million years.
Since their past affinities have already been revealed and the supreme realm has first been established, Śākyamuni—[at this point, the text continues].

Maitreya previously preached this sutra desiring that, before he himself attains Buddhahood, he might swiftly fulfill the vows of sentient beings, providing them with support and protection so they may reach the Western Land.

Furthermore, because sentient beings of middling and inferior capacities are prone to falling back from their practice, if Maitreya has not yet descended to attain Buddhahood, at what time shall these sentient beings behold the Buddha? If...
If one does not take birth in the Western Pure Land early on, once fallen into the three miserable realms, there will be no hope of emerging.
Often, when the assembly at the Dragon Flower Tree has dispersed, sentient beings have yet to regain their human bodies.

Thus, with Śākyamuni already gone and Maitreya not yet arrived, this sutra alone is able to pull forth all sentient beings from the abode of suffering and bring them to fulfillment; its grace is exceedingly profound. This is the path.
This is indeed most expedient. Now, the sages of the Three Teachings arose in succession to save the world; responding to the times and according to the seasons, each established their own system.
If one says that there is no second path in the world and no dual intention in the sages, then when speaking in accordance with the nature of reality, the single True Suchness runs through them all.
Whether among gods or humans, within the midst of those who have realized birth-and-death and those who have not, one seeks...
If one wishes to be entirely free from all defects, there are hundreds of thousands of skillful means, yet the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is foremost among them.
Why need one rely on the supernatural powers of the Buddha-dharma? By attaining birth in that land through this very practice, one obtains the essence of all supernatural powers.
Why necessarily seek the golden elixir of the Daoist school? This very lotus flower washes away all habitual attachments to the golden elixir.
Why necessarily seek the principles of the Confucian school? This very state of "the one mind undistracted" shatters all obstacles to the study of principles.
One attains its root, while the three teachings are all but branches and leaves. The root is the single thought-moment of mind.

Yet, one must first perceive the Buddha and perceive the mind before realizing that it is neither mind nor Buddha; thus, one naturally traverses the three teachings in all directions and enters and exits the Dragon Flower Assembly.
Alas! Mañjuśrī realized the principle of the Western Land and took his place at the head of the honored assembly, while Maitreya...
As for those with the capacity for rebirth in the Pure Land, this [sūtra] is ranked second. Among the infinite multitude of ordinary beings and sages, who would dare to disparage this scripture?
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Gandhahasti.

*Kandahati* means "unresting" in this [Chinese] context. Having already developed faith in the Pure Land but not yet having been reborn there, one who can take "unresting" as their resolve will naturally tread upon it step by step.
The Bodhisattva Constant Diligence (Sadā-vīrya):
"Diligent" means he is not coarse; "progressive" means he does not regress. Being constantly thus, he is able to use the Dharma of the Pure Land to deliver himself and others.
Together with such great bodhisattvas as these—
taking these four honored ones as representative of all bodhisattvas—
and accompanied by Śakra-devānām-indra and an immeasurable assembly of devas, [the Buddha was present].
Śakra-devānām-indra—here translated as "The Lord of Devas"—is the one commonly referred to in the world as the Jade Emperor of the Celestial Palace.
Regarding the "immeasurable devas": the Jade Emperor resides in the Trāyastriṃśa (Heaven of the Thirty-three) Palace atop Mount Sumeru.
This palace has four sides, with eight kings on each side; collectively, they are called the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Below the Trāyastriṃśa heaven is Mount Sumeru.
On the terraces, there are the Four Great Heavenly Kings of the East, West, South, and North, who preside over forty kinds of minor deities.

Above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, those who dwell in the void are the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens; these, together with the Trāyastriṃśa, constitute [the Realm of Desire].
The Four Kings are called the devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Beyond this, there are no longer women; these are called the devas of the dhyāna realm (*dhyānadhātu*).
Beyond this, there is no longer a physical body; these are called the devas of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Among the three realms, the desire realm is the most diverse.

Those in the formless realm have no bodies, yet through being moved by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*prabhāva*), they manifest forms to listen to the Dharma. This is beyond the reach of thought.

"Those who can reach [this]" refers to the great assembly. "Great Assembly" generally indicates all those capable of hearing the Dharma within the heavens above and the world below the desire realm, including dragons, spirits, ghosts, immortals, and other beings.
"Together" (俱) means collectively; it signifies that they enter the Buddha’s assembly along with the sages.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra.
Regarding the phrase "the Buddha addressed": because his compassionate heart was moved with such urgency, he did not wait for a question.
"From here, toward the west..."
"From" (*cong*) means "by way of. "This" (*shi*) refers generally to this Sahā world. "The West" (*xi fang*) means going toward the western direction.
To point specifically to one direction is to fixate upon a single quarter; only when the spirit and will are focused and tranquil can one initiate the efficacy of practice and achieve success.
It must be called "the West" because the Sahā world is situated directly opposite the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
"Eastward. This has no other meaning.
"Passing beyond ten million *koṭis* of Buddha-fields.
A *koṭi* is ten million; alternatively, it is said that one hundred thousand is a *koṭi*. A "Buddha-field" (*buddhakṣetra*) refers to a single Great Trichiliocosm. A single Great [Trichiliocosm]...
Among a thousand [worlds], one is presided over by a Buddha for the purpose of transformation.
"World" (*loka*) refers to temporal divisions, namely the past, present, and future. "Sphere" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial divisions, namely the eight directions.
It is that which is above and below. Within a single radiance of mind, empty space appears; within empty space, the wind-circle appears;
within the wind-circle, the earth-element appears. Once the divisions of earth are established, the divisions of time arise accordingly;
thus it is called a "world. The radiance of mind is immeasurable, empty space is immeasurable, and all worlds are likewise immeasurable.
Therefore, there exists the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) and various worlds to the west of that Ultimate Bliss;
there exists the Eastern Sahā World and various worlds to the east of that Sahā World.
Above the uppermost, below the lowermost, to the south of the southernmost, and to the north of the northernmost—there is not one direction that does not likewise possess its own variety [of worlds].
There are various worlds. That which we inhabit is named Saha. "Saha" means "endurance";

it signifies that sentient beings endure suffering. Out of great compassion, the Buddha spoke of a world beyond hundreds of thousands of millions of lands in order to enable sentient beings to fly forth across this Saha world with a single thought-moment.

Furthermore, those of the Two Vehicles do not transcend the trichiliocosm; they may dwell in the Brahma worlds or be confined within the intermediate realms, limited by their heavenly merits to a single world-system.
As for the powers of elixirs and immortals, they remain within the realm of desire. Reflect upon this with an impartial mind: their meanness and insignificance are beyond words.
It was the Buddha, amidst the great dream of sentient beings, who called out to them and declared: "Beyond ten thousand myriads of koṭis..."
There is a world within the earth. Alas! Only now do I realize that there exists a separate heaven and earth.
○ The wheel of mind-nature is simply the single thought of a person. Within the wheel of mind-nature appears the wheel of space; within the wheel of space appears the immeasurable wheel of wind;
within one wheel of wind appears one wheel of gold, which is the underside of the wheel of earth. The wheel of gold...
Above appears a wheel of fire; above the wheel of fire appears a wheel of water;
and atop the wheel of water emerge various mountains and various continents—these being the upper surface of the earth-wheel. Among them, the most exquisite and lofty is Mount Sumeru.
Upon the slopes of the mountains, the sun and moon revolve in their coming and going. The low-lying regions of the earth-wheel are called the hells;
the high elevations of the earth-wheel, such as the summit and terraces of Mount Sumeru, are all called celestial palaces.

Beyond the summit of Mount Sumeru, there are four classes of devas who dwell supported by space; these, together with the Trāyastriṃśa heaven atop Mount Sumeru and the terraces of Mount Sumeru, constitute [the celestial realms].
The King of Heaven refers to the Six Desire Heavens. Above these are three tiers of heavens called the First Dhyāna.
From this First Dhyāna down to the hells, this is termed a "small world.
One thousand such small worlds are called a "small chiliocosm," which is presided over by the Heavenly Kings of the Second Dhyāna. One thousand such small chiliocosms are called...

It is called the intermediate chiliocosm (*madhyama-sāhasra-lokadhātu*). It is presided over by the celestial kings of the third dhyāna. When one thousand such intermediate chiliocosms are accumulated, it is named the great chiliocosm (*mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*).

It is presided over by the celestial kings of the fourth dhyāna. Within the fourth dhyāna heavens, there dwell the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the five heavens of Non-Returners (*anāgāmin*);
yet the celestial kings do not see them, nor do they know of them. That which is above the fourth dhyāna is named...
Empty space. Although the soul-consciousness remains, the physical form has perished; it likewise exists within the great trichiliocosm.
Such a great trichiliocosm is called a single Buddha-land. The Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha is one great trichiliocosm; the Sahā world of Śākyamuni is also one great trichiliocosm.
Within one great trichiliocosm, ten billion suns and moons appear, and ten billion transformations appear.
The Buddhas—pure and impure, long and short, hidden and manifest, appearing and disappearing—reflect one another to form a pattern, like lamps in the clouds or the moon in the water.
These worlds are layered upon one another, termed the "Ocean of Worlds.

This ocean of worlds is infinitely repeated and inexhaustible, arising from the "World-Seed" (*jagat-kula*). This world-seed is infinitely repeated and inexhaustible, arising from the fragrance of the lotus.
Within the ocean of water, within this Flower Treasury (Padmakośa), there are various adornments, which are called the "Flower Adornment" (Avataṃsaka).
The lotus flower is one, like the true mind; the worlds are many, like deluded thoughts. Yet this very lotus flower is neither true nor deluded.
It is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
While this generally refers to the Western Quarter, there are actually many worlds therein, with varying degrees of beauty and ugliness.

By specifically designating it as "Ultimate Bliss," one’s devotion becomes singular and decisive, eliminating any further concern for confusion or error. ○ The people of the world take India (the West Heaven) to be the Western Quarter.

"Pure Land. This is not so. "Western Heaven" refers to the land of India (Tianzhu), which is the western direction within this Sahā world-system, not the western direction outside of the Sahā world-system;
one must not misunderstand this. The pleasures of the human realm and the heavens do not equal those of Amitābha’s land.
The bliss of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the two vehicles does not equal that of Amitābha’s land. [This is true for] all Buddhas...
Within other lands, there may be conditions that have not yet aligned, or merit cultivated with regression; thus, although they possess various kinds of bliss, it does not equal the land of Amitābha.

For those born in the land of Amitābha, flowers bloom spontaneously, they see the Buddha spontaneously, they hear the wondrous Dharma spontaneously, they develop supernormal powers spontaneously, they deliver sentient beings spontaneously, and they achieve the Way spontaneously.
The spiritual energy is serene and solitary, free from all further entanglements; when one is perfectly integrated within the single mirror, only then is there true bliss.
In that land dwells a Buddha named Amitābha.
The Buddha is the sovereign teacher who transforms beings within a single world-system; therefore, he is listed first.
Furthermore, Amitābha Buddha specializes in teaching people to attain rebirth by means of reciting his name; therefore, he is listed with particular urgency.
*A* means "non-"; *mita* means "measure"; and *buddha* means "awakened. Awakening is the luminosity of the mind. *Amitā-*...
Amida Buddha attained Buddhahood through the light of the immeasurable mind; we too shall practice mindfulness of the Buddha through the light of the immeasurable mind.
By reciting "Amida" while mindful of Amida, every thought-moment returns to the immeasurable.
The radiance of the mind is like a single great round mirror, filling all of space, without distinction of "that" or "this"—I take hold of it.
Thus, it is entirely my mirror. When a Buddha accords with this, it is entirely the Buddha’s mirror.
Using the "I" within the Buddha’s mirror to contemplate the Buddha within my mirror; using the Buddha within my mirror to deliver the "I" within the Buddha’s mirror.
He is currently preaching the Dharma.
As for "the present," it is not like Śākyamuni, who dwelt in the world for over eighty years before suddenly passing into the past;
nor is it like Maitreya, who will descend after the passage of thousands of millions of years and thus remains in the future. Sentient beings today—
One attains liberation. Sentient beings today urgently seek liberation; the Dharma is preached today—is this not the divine panacea for the emergency of the present age?
Although it is said to be "ten million billion," it is but the light of the single mind.
Wherever the thoughts of the mind move, there is immediately a resonance within the mirror of the mind. The heart-light of all Buddhas permeates the three [realms].
Worldly beings do not awaken and remain stalled in the present; to transform that which is stalled into penetration is the wondrous function of the Unsurpassed King of Physicians.
As the later text says: "Since attaining Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed until now. It further says: "I now make this vow: if it were my current life... Alas!

To miss the present is to err once and inevitably incur a hundred errors. Human life— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "Human life" (人命). The translation reflects the available portion.*
While breathing, each should exert themselves accordingly. Śāriputra,
that which was previously my "I-hearing" (ahaṃśravaṇa) is precisely Ānanda’s "I," and it manifests the "I" of all who recite the sūtras.
This Śāriputra is none other than the very mind of Śāriputra; it awakens the minds of all sentient beings, which is why he calls out and summons them again and again.
Alas! As the moon reflects in a thousand rivers, the principle pervades both the ordinary and the sage.
If we were to clearly understand this function of the Buddha, how could we not shed tears of profound gratitude and contemplate how to repay the Buddha’s kindness?
Why is that land named "Ultimate Bliss"? Because the sentient beings in that country are free from all forms of suffering and experience only various joys,
it is therefore called "Ultimate Bliss."

"Sentient beings" refers to those who come into existence through the combination of the various aggregates (*skandha*). These "various aggregates" are the five aggregates. One aggregate, that of form (*rūpa*), is called external phenomena;
feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are called the internal mind. They are thus bound and led by these five aggregates.
One realizes the essence of the Buddha while becoming a sentient being, and is not constrained or dragged about by the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

One realizes the essence of the Buddha while remaining a sentient being. Regarding "various sufferings": these are the three sufferings, the five sufferings, and the eight sufferings. When there is suffering, it is called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);

when pleasure is impermanent, it is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); and when one cannot abide in neutral states, it is called the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). These are the three sufferings.
The suffering of birth is the extreme state of turbidity. The suffering of old age is the ultimate state of exhaustion and infirmity.

The suffering of illness is the depth of pain and itching. The suffering of death is the disarray of the spirit and the pulses. The suffering of the five aggregates is the conflict with one's environment. These are the five sufferings.
When the suffering of suffering itself is expanded into four types, they constitute the eight sufferings; namely, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
The suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, and the suffering of the proliferation of the five aggregates.
Regarding "all pleasures," this refers to both worldly and supramundane pleasures. The radiance of the seven treasures and the ability to travel by flight are worldly pleasures.
To recollect the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha and join with the assembly of the virtuous is the bliss of transcending the world.

To never retreat from Bodhi and realize the stage of the "one more birth" (Ekajātipratibaddha) is the supreme bliss of transcending the world. Upon reaching this state, one experiences that which is not experienced; this is called *samyaksamādhi* (right reception).
To experience that which is not experienced is the realm of awakening; to experience that which is experienced is the realm of non-awakening. This is the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The world encompasses both; the eternal, quiescent, and radiant land (nitya-prabhāsvara-kṣetra) is identical with the realm of common cohabitation (sahā-loka). It includes both the holy and the ordinary, and those of all three capacities may proceed together.
There is no one whom the Buddha does not reach out his hand to rescue.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the land of Ultimate Bliss, there are sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees,
all of which are completely surrounded by the four precious substances.
Other worlds are bounded by the Iron Ring Mountains as their barriers;

the Land of Ultimate Bliss, however, demarcates its boundaries with jeweled railings, jeweled nets, and jeweled trees, merely following the formal conventions of a buddha-field. These four jewels are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
For this reason, that land is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
As soon as one enters the Western Quarter, one first beholds the radiance of layered, multifold clusters of jewels;
thereupon, one suddenly realizes that both that realm and this world are all like reflections appearing in a mirror. This is the foremost bliss never before seen in one's entire life.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds made of the seven treasures, brought forth by the power of pure karma. They are level, straight, and luminous; thus, there are no dangers from mountains or seas.
There are only these ponds of treasure and pavilions, their splendors reflecting one another. As for the "seven-treasure ponds," this refers to ponds of treasure located in seven places.
The water of eight virtues fills its midst.
As for these eight virtues: first, it is limpid and pure; second, it is cool and refreshing; third, it is sweet and delicious; fourth, it is light and soft; fifth, it is moistening and lustrous.
Sixth, it brings harmony. Seventh, it removes hunger and thirst. Eighth, it nurtures the sense faculties.
The bottom of the pond is entirely covered with golden sand;
as for silt and mud, these are produced by evil karma. Because the spirit is clear and manifest, and virtuous karma is firm and pure, such a manifestation is brought forth.
It is of golden sand.
The stairways on its four sides are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Above it are pavilions, likewise adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, red pearls, and agate.
Vaidūrya is not a stone resin; sphatika is not mineral pitch; musāragalva is not a veined stone;
and lohitamukti is not the essence of an oyster. These names of objects from this land are used to manifest the characteristics of objects in that land;
yet the actual objects of that land cannot truly be compared to those of this land.

In the pond were lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels; those that were blue emitted a blue light, those that were yellow a yellow light, those that were red a red light, and those that were white a white light—subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure.
Those born in that land take lotus flowers as their parents; therefore, it is praised in detail. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there are no women at all.
When women are reborn there, they all become men. Thus, people are all born within lotus flowers.
The flesh-and-blood wombs of this turbid world are heavy, coarse, foul, and impure; therefore, the light of a person’s merit and wisdom [is obscured therein].
Within the mother’s womb, it is entirely lost; yet upon birth, it becomes increasingly active.
In the lotus-womb of the Pure Land, which is subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure, the light of a person’s merit and wisdom suddenly shines forth brilliantly within the Buddha-nature;
yet upon birth, it progressively transcends all. Among the palaces of the various devas, there is also...
The lotus flower. However, it arises solely through the retribution of merit and lacks a definitive cause; thus, it is finite and not infinite.

If the reflection of a single thought-moment of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) falls upon the heart-mirror of Amitābha Buddha, the spiritual intelligence awakens and both cause and effect become efficacious.
One will naturally be able to enter the ranks of the sages with eternal clarity and brilliance. The Lotus Flower.
It emanates from the mind. Whenever an ordinary person gives rise to a single thought of aspiration to go [there], a single lotus bud immediately appears within the Western Pool of Seven Jewels.
If one can cultivate and practice this moment after moment, then the precious veins will be deeply contained and the fragrant breezes will flourish.
○ "As large as a chariot wheel" means it is commensurate with the body. As for the bodies of the various devas and nāgas...
It extends for several hundred *li*. Once one is born into the flower-wheel (*puṣpa-cakra*), it can never contract back to a smaller size.
The dimensions of the bodies of Bodhisattvas in the Pure Land are inconceivable; how could they be restricted to a wheel of only a few feet?
One should know that all phenomena differ according to the measure of the mind (*citta-pramāṇa*); it is the spiritual intelligence that summons [the manifestation], not the Tathāgata.
There are those who limit people by external conditions. When the spirit of mindfulness awakens and the radiance of light intermingles, the mind itself is the flower;
it is a state of tranquil oneness. Thus, though the body has not yet departed, the spiritual intelligence already dwells within the flower.
Śāriputra, the land of Sukhāvatī is thus adorned with the accomplishment of such meritorious virtues.
This is the adornment of the jeweled ponds and lotus calyxes within the boundaries of that land.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that buddha-land, celestial music constantly plays;
the musical instruments of the West sound spontaneously without being struck. This is because it is adorned above by the splendor of precious sounds.
The ground is made of gold;
this is adorned below by the radiance of jewels.
Six times throughout the day and night, celestial *mandārava* flowers rain down.

The hours of Xu (戌), Zi (子), and Yin (寅) constitute the three periods of night; the hours of Chen (辰), Wu (午), and Shen (申) constitute the three periods of day. The practitioner observes these as the divisions of time.
Now, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is entirely a realm of pure radiance; how could it rely upon the sun and moon to distinguish day from night?
It is merely by the opening and closing of the lotus flowers. "Rain" means to descend. *Mandārava* is white in color.
Previously, the spatial dimensions were adorned with sounds and lights; here, the temporal divisions are adorned with fragrances and lights.
Transcending all limits of verticality and horizontality, they are freely manifested within the precious mind.
The sentient beings in that land are called "sentient beings," yet they are in truth bodhisattvas.
Every morning at dawn, they...

During the first watch of the day, each person filled their robe-sleeve with various exquisite flowers to make offerings to ten trillion Buddhas in other directions (the character *gèi* is pronounced *gé*).
At the time of rebirth, their minds flew forth to those ten trillion Buddha-lands; after rebirth, their bodies likewise flew.

He wondrously entered a hundred trillion buddha-lands. "Yiji" (衣裓) refers to the lap or hem of a robe. By means of his miraculous transformations and divided bodies, he reached the presence of all the Buddhas;
thus, in a single morning, he was able to make offerings everywhere throughout those hundred trillion lands.
At the very hour of eating, he returned to his native land;
having departed at dawn, he had already returned. His ethereal form manifested with such clarity that the variations in quantity or distance were truly insufficient to burden his mind.
They ate their meals and practiced walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). Some took the joy of *dhyāna* as their food; some took seeing forms and hearing fragrances as their food;
and some consumed transformed (*nirmāṇa*) food and drink. After eating, they practiced walking meditation; whether moving or still, all entered the Buddha’s sphere of activity.
Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with such meritorious qualities;
this is the adornment of the Buddha’s own body and mind, which are sovereign and capable of making offerings.
Furthermore,
Śāriputra, that land is constantly filled with various wondrous birds of diverse colors.
The following names of birds are for the most part metaphorical. The various birds of that country have no fixed forms;
they cannot be conceived of in terms of size, color intensity, or shading.
The white crane, the peacock, the parrot, the śāri, the kalaviṅka, and the saṃjīva bird.
The śāri is a species such as the sarus crane. The kalaviṅka is a divine bird of wondrous song. The saṃjīva is the "double-life" bird.
Each has one foot and one wing; they live when together and die when separated. The *Erya* calls them "wing-to-wing" birds (*biyi*), while the common world refers to them as "double-headed.
Bound by the bitter entanglements of affection, their karmic retribution results in this avian form. This manifestation appears in that land, though it is identical in shape to those found here.
These various birds, throughout the six periods of day and night, produce harmonious and elegant sounds;
these sounds expound and clarify the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and other such dharmas.

There are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*): the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), as well as the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the path (*mārga*).
The five faculties are faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The five powers are those which are developed from the faculties.
The seven factors of enlightenment are: first, investigation of phenomena; second, energy; third, joy; fourth, tranquility; fifth, equanimity; sixth, concentration; and seventh, mindfulness.
The eightfold path consists of: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
When the sentient beings of that land hear this sound, they all recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Therefore, those who skillfully utilize what they hear find that all sounds are the voice of the Buddha.
As for the Dharma, it is that by which the Buddha attained Buddhahood. As for the Sangha, it consists of the Bodhisattvas and the Śrāvakas.
Śāriputra, do not say that these birds are actually born as a result of their karmic retribution for sins. Why is this?
In that buddha-field, there are no three evil realms of existence.
The three evil realms refer to the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals. Someone may ask:

"In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there are no women, no asuras, no immortals, and no māras or non-Buddhists; the physical realm is level and serene. Therefore, the burdens of war, water, fire, wife, children, and household have no basis to arise.
Why, then, do you speak only of the absence of the evil realms? The answer is: The preceding text states "no... [and continues as follows].
A single phrase—“all manner of suffering”—encompasses it all.
Śāriputra, in that buddha-land, even the name of the evil realms does not exist, let alone their actual presence.
All these various birds are transformations produced by Amitābha Buddha, intended to cause the sounds of the Dharma to flow forth.
It is not substantially existent, Śāriputra.

In that Buddha-land, when a gentle breeze stirs the rows of jewel trees and the precious netting, they produce a subtle and wondrous sound, like hundreds of thousands of kinds of music playing simultaneously. Those who hear this sound naturally all [attain...]
They give rise to thoughts of mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Previously, the manifested auspicious birds inspired people to mindfully recollect the Buddha and sentient beings preached the Dharma; this was already a wondrous and exquisite creation.
Now, once again, the sounds of the non-sentient preaching the Dharma are transcribed, suddenly like the gentle breeze upon a jeweled net.
When reading to this point—"At that time, [the wind] blows and moves"—how could one possibly cease making the vow to be reborn there? Someone may ask:

There is "recollection of the Buddha through the true mark" (*lakṣaṇa-buddhānusmṛti*), which is the profound contemplation of the Buddha’s principle. There is "recollection of the Buddha through visualization" (*saṃjñā-buddhānusmṛti*), which is entering the concentration of the Western Land.

There is "recollection of the Buddha by contemplating an image" (*pratimā-buddhānusmṛti*), which is generating reverence toward an image. There is "recollection of the Buddha by holding the name" (*nāmadheya-buddhānusmṛti*), which is the [recitation of the] characters...
The phrasing is clearly correct. When sentient beings in the Western Land recite the Buddha’s name, how do they recite it? The answer is:
without being hindered by names, one gives rise to the true mark (dharmatā). Entering meditative concentration within sound, sound itself is light.
The four types of mindfulness of the Buddha are all, in fact, one single type of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Śāriputra, that buddha-field is adorned with such accomplished merits and graces;
this is the adornment of practice, inspired by the appropriate time and season.
Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha?

Having already explained the name of the Buddha-field, I shall now again explain the title of the Buddha’s body. Those who speak of the Pure Land as being solely the mind may not necessarily be able to travel spiritually through the Buddha-fields;
those who speak of the Self-nature Amitābha may not necessarily be able to measure their capacity to be equal to the Buddha’s body.
If one speaks with the mouth but does not practice with the mind, how can there be the joy of rebirth?
Śāriputra, the light of that Buddha is immeasurable;
the fundamental ground of the minds of all sentient beings is also immeasurable in its luminosity. All Buddhas realize this.
The fundamental ground of the minds of sentient beings is originally one; thus, their radiant light is equally immeasurable.
However, while the immeasurable light of all Buddhas is difficult for sentient beings to perceive, the immeasurable light of Amitābha Buddha is easy for them to perceive.
This is because the ripening of their causes and conditions differs. Such is the nature of the causes and conditions of Amitābha Buddha.
Since he has already matured sentient beings, his guidance through immeasurable rays of light is certain, most certain,
and beyond all doubt.
He illuminates the lands of the ten directions without any obstruction.
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, there are various Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Sumerus, and great oceans—chaotic and solid obstructions that hinder the human mind.
Only when the ground of the mind is transformed into radiance does it become translucent and free.
Since the Buddha takes radiance as his entire being, he illuminates the ten directions everywhere; yet sentient beings cling stubbornly to solidity and thus remain obstructed.
Therefore, it is difficult to perceive even a single Buddha. However, speaking from the perspective of the Buddha himself, there is only radiance and no obstruction whatsoever;
within this expanse of radiance, all obstructions are themselves radiance.
One who understands this principle will surely transcend the stages and grounds at the time of rebirth, attaining certainty of mind.
For this reason, he is named Amitābha.
This refers to his immeasurability in terms of light.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the lifespan of that Buddha, as well as that of his people, shall endure for immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Therefore, he is named Amitābha.
This explains his "immeasurability" (*amita*) in terms of his lifespan. *Asaṃkhyeya* means "innumerable. *Kalpa* refers to a long period of time.
Śāriputra, since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed until now.
This word "now" is spoken in reference to this present Bhadrakalpa of the Sahā world; thus, while his time is immeasurable, only ten kalpas have appeared.
Thus, there are no sentient beings who have been mired in ignorance for kalpas who do not rely upon the guidance of that light.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats;
they cannot be known by means of calculation. The assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise so numerous (the word "shù" is pronounced with a rising tone).

Those of the two vehicles who possess the seeds [of liberation] do not take birth in the Pure Land. As for the Arhats of the Pure Land, they have for the most part already resolved their minds upon the Great Bodhisattva path;
having briefly realized the stage of a Śrāvaka, they immediately ascend to the rank of a Mahāsattva. When the light reaches them, their bodies become like shadows and echoes.
Śāriputra, that buddha-field is adorned with such perfected merits and graces.
This is the adornment of the sovereign and its retinue, characterized by exquisite brilliance and longevity.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, all those beings born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are *avivarti*—*a* meaning "non-" and *vivarti* meaning "retrogression.
While practicing here [in this world], one encounters much suffering and many demons;
like a single hair in the wind, one cannot maintain self-mastery. But by being born once in Ultimate Bliss, one immediately attains the stage of non-retrogression.

Among them, there were many who were in their last birth before attaining Buddhahood; their number was so vast that it could not be known by calculation, but can only be described as immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).

One who is "in the position of succession" (kṣetra-parigraha) refers to an Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva (samyak-saṃbodhi-bodhisattva) who awaits the opportune time to attain Buddhahood in another world-system.
From the human stage up to Buddhahood, the number of births and lifetimes through which they advance and retreat is unknowable.

Only those beings in the Pure Land are able to bypass many lifetimes and enter directly into the position of succession in another world in a single lifetime; this is said to be because their conditions are superior and the kalpa is long.
Śāriputra, there are many who have achieved vast success.
When sentient beings hear this, they should make a vow, vowing to be born in that land.
Amitābha Buddha is called the "King of Vows," for among all Buddhas, his vow to deliver sentient beings is the most supreme.

First, sentient beings accord with the Buddha’s vows by making the aspiration for rebirth. Like a magnet attracting iron, like a lamp emitting light, or like a drumstick striking a drum, there is mutual resonance and response;
the wondrous vow becomes the occasion for awakening, becoming clear and resonant in every thought-moment.
There is no rebirth that is not thus clear and resonant.
Why is this? It is because one has been able to assemble together with such superior and virtuous people in a single place.

Indeed, the past is difficult to pursue and the future is unfathomable; to undergo suffering in the present while drawing down calamity for the future is what causes the greatest unease in human hearts.
One must only diligently uphold the Buddha’s name to be born early in the Western Land.
In this place, those who gaze up in reverence behold the Tathāgata; those who gather here are none other than the most virtuous.
How wondrous it is that those illuminated by his radiance are inspired and brought to fulfillment!
Śāriputra, one cannot be born in that land through meager roots of goodness or causes and conditions of merit.

It is because all their practices do not take mindfulness of the Buddha as the cause, and their general mindfulness of the Buddha does not take the diligent upholding of the four characters as the condition;
thus, they lack any sense of restraint regarding the timing for the Pure Land, and consequently, their goodness and merit are not great.
Furthermore, the light of that Buddha is immeasurable, while sentient beings seek it with limited merit and virtue;
as these two are so vastly different, it is therefore impossible.
Śāriputra, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing it said that among the sentient beings of the six realms,
each has both male and female forms, are able to believe in the Buddha with their hearts, they may be called "good.
To hear it said that Amitābha Buddha exists means to hear from others about the realm of Amitābha Buddha.
"Grasping and holding the name" means to grasp and maintain these four characters of Amitābha Buddha’s name. "Grasping" means that the mind focuses on the four characters without withdrawing.
"Holding" means that the mouth recites the four characters without interruption. [The character] ○ represents the Name.
Beyond this, there is no further Amitābha. That Amitābha is Amitābha—these four characters encompass it all.

The great name of myriad virtues; the myriad virtues are the great name. To invoke virtue by means of the name, a single phrase contains it all. Within that single phrase, what more could possibly be lacking?
Indeed, a mind that lacks nothing is itself "immeasurable" (amita). It is itself "A."
This is Amitābha. These roots of goodness and merit are truly beyond measure of quantity.
It is like a single drop of water cast into the great ocean; every drop of water cast into the great ocean is such that not a single drop is not the ocean.
○ Indeed, there is no Chan apart from the Buddha, and no contemplation apart from mindfulness. Thus, to mindfully recite the Buddha's name is itself...
This is Zen meditation (*chán*). It is not necessary to form a separate conceptualization of "Zen meditation.

If, while reciting the Buddha’s name, you observe, "Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name?"—reciting and observing at once—this results in two thoughts. It is better simply to continue reciting directly.
The word "clinging" (*zhí*) is the sickness of all practitioners. It is the reason why all sentient beings cannot [attain liberation].
To become a Buddha is to be burdened by the attachments of one's own sentiments. However, when a fever has run deep, gypsum can be used;
once the internal organs are saturated, saltpeter and magnesia can be applied. A single flavor of bland simplicity is insufficient to raise the dead and restore life;

therefore, one uses attachment to break through attachment, so that the illness may suddenly vanish. When attachment reaches its limit, the light of the mind is revealed; and when the light of the mind is revealed—
The Buddha’s light shines upon them, yet practitioners do not perceive it; nevertheless, the Buddha clearly discerns it all. Furthermore, how could practitioners truly be unaware?
It is simply that if they cultivate a single mind free from distraction, they will naturally obtain a new set of bones.
For those who practice the Way, it is well to undergo this one period of hardship.
Whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days— generally speaking,
"holding the name" refers to constant and diligent practice; specifically, it points to a single day or seven days.
This refers to courageous and diligent effort. It is like refining elixirs, using either gentle fire or fierce fire;

with single-mindedness and without distraction, though the mind is devoid of both the real and the false, the real and the false manifest. As the real and the false arise alternately, one cannot find a way back to the source. Thus, the real and the false...

All these are delusions; they are the cause of the mind’s confusion. To contemplate immeasurable Buddhas with an immeasurable mind, no longer conceiving thoughts of the finite or the infinite—this is what is called being undisturbed.
When that person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings, appears before them.

"The moment of approaching death" refers to the single thought-moment immediately preceding death. That the Buddha appears before them is the response evoked by their single-mindedness and lack of distraction.
Indeed, my mind and the Buddha’s mind are like mirrors reflecting one another; thus, to recite the Buddha's name with single-mindedness is—
The eastern mirror entering the western mirror is like seeing the Buddha at the end of one's life; the western mirror entering the eastern mirror is likewise so.
Although they enter one another, there is no trace of coming or going; it is merely the mutual connection of their radiance.
○ The reason why all practitioners are unable to reach a definitive conclusion is that they lack a firm grasp at the moment of death. Although...
Furthermore, when the vital energies and channels become clear and pure, and the incense in the burner ascends upward, it often reaches the realms of the celestial immortals;
yet from this point downward, it becomes increasingly desolate.

There are those who see the fiery chariots and the hell-wardens, and there are those who mistakenly enter halls, buildings, gardens, and groves, only for these to transform into the evil paths of existence. Only this *Amitābha Sūtra* alone—
The four characters "at the time of the end of life" are presented like a single clap of spring thunder that startles all hibernating creatures;
there is no one who possesses the Dharma-body of the life of wisdom who does not have a path for emergence. This principle is difficult to hear, and this capacity is difficult to awaken.
Now that you have heard this principle and awakened this capacity, can you not exert yourselves for the sake of your kinsmen throughout three lifetimes?
When such a person reaches the end of life, their mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
"The end of life" refers to the single thought-moment of actually casting off the retribution of the body. "The mind is not inverted" means that right mindfulness manifests before them.
An onlooker who sees that this person’s mind is not inverted can believe with certainty that this person has already attained rebirth in the Pure Land.
○ To hear the sutra and make a vow; to make a vow and hold the Name; to hold the Name and see the Buddha;
to see the Buddha and attain rebirth—these five stages are mutually dependent, a natural sequence. Yet people today have their spiritual pulse inverted.
One will not attain rebirth; there is merely the merit of holding the Name, yet one does not reach the state of single-mindedness without distraction.
Consequently, those who are muddled and distracted fill the world, and the Compassionate Ferry remains empty, providing no salvation.
○ Not making vows arises from not hearing the sutra; not attaining rebirth arises from not making vows. Furthermore, there is greed for seeing [the Buddha].
The Buddha is weary of those who are indolent in upholding the Name, for they turn this single gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha into a stagnant and lifeless state.
Alas! The supreme elixir has turned to putrid decay; the true jewel net lies buried in vain within the silt and sand.

This is because the mind and spirit are unable to gather in perfect concentration. Regarding those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name: in every thought-moment, their majestic spiritual power is entirely identical to that of our Buddha.
Vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as empty space, within the radiance of such a mind, demonic interference can never occur.
Śāriputra, it is because I see this benefit that I speak these words: if there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should make a vow to be born in that land.
One should repeatedly encourage the making of vows; these are the mind’s vows and the Buddha’s vows, their lights intermingling to serve as the ticket for rebirth in the Pure Land.
To claim that the single gate of Nianfo (Buddha-recitation) is merely a means to entice the common and inferior is, in truth, a sin equal to slandering the Buddha.
Śāriputra, just as I now praise the inconceivable benefits of the merit of Amitābha Buddha—
whereby manifest virtue is called "merit" (功) and non-manifest merit is called "virtue" (德)— these merits and virtues are beneficial to...
Sentient beings call this "benefit. It cannot be conceived by the mind, nor can it be discussed by the mouth.
To speak of the merits of Amitābha Buddha is to speak of immeasurable merits. He who praises them is Śākyamuni Buddha.
Those who offer praise do not stop with Śākyamuni Buddha alone; taking myself as an example for them, it is said that they are "like" him.
In the eastern direction, there is also the Buddha Akṣobhya, the Buddha Sumerukūṭa, the Buddha Mahāsumeru, and the Buddha Sumeruprabha.
Ghosadatta Buddha. Thus, there are Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (the character for "shu" is pronounced "cu").
The Sahā world lies to the east of Sukhāvatī; yet, to the east of the Sahā world, the worlds are likewise immeasurable.
The Land of Ultimate Bliss lies to the west of this Sahā world. Yet, to the west of that Land of Ultimate Bliss, worlds extend infinitely once more.
People of the world possess narrow vision and know only the six directions;

how could they know that beyond these worlds there are worlds, each with a Tathāgata of Great Wisdom and Radiance who, out of compassion for eternal kalpas, exhorts people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha? ○
Akṣobhya: this is translated as "Immovable. Sumeru: the name of a mountain; this is translated as "Wondrously High" (Miaogao).
It is the largest mountain at the very center of the world-system. The Buddha’s name is derived from the mountain’s name to signify the wondrous loftiness of his virtuous marks and characteristics.
In each of their respective lands, they extend the mark of the broad and long tongue, completely covering the trichiliocosm.
This tongue-mark is immeasurable because the bodily marks are immeasurable; the bodily marks are immeasurable because the mental marks are immeasurable.
Teaching the Dharma everywhere, the Dharma fills the great trichiliocosm, which is why it is called "completely covering. Yet, as for the Buddha’s body—

Manifesting lands; manifesting buddha-fields within bodies; manifesting bodies within bodies; and manifesting lands within lands—his tongue covering the great trichiliocosm—there has never been a time when these things were not actually so.
I speak these words of sincerity:
among all sentient beings, there are those who hear this sutra yet do not believe it;

there are those within the monastic community who recite this throughout their lives as a daily liturgy, yet fail to give rise to even a single thought of seeking rebirth [in the Pure Land]. They have merely borrowed the aspirational texts of the ancients and followed established custom.

To recite [the scriptures] while being like one who counts another's treasures while possessing not a single coin himself—perceiving phenomena as external to the mind, flowing away without returning—alas!
Such people are as numerous as the surging waters.
"You sentient beings, you should believe in this Sutra on the Immeasurable Life, which extols inconceivable merit and is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
"Extols" means to proclaim its excellence. "Inconceivable merit" refers to Amitābha by way of his Name.

This refers to the deliverance of sentient beings. All Buddhas—the Buddhas of the six directions as well as Śākyamuni Buddha—protect and keep in mind those who believe in the merits of Amitābha and make the vow to be reborn there.

Even if various internal or external māras should inflict harm upon them, all Tathāgatas constantly bestow their protective mindfulness, empowering them with their majestic spiritual power to bring them to fulfillment. This is the fifteenth [vow].
"Name" refers to the title of the sutra; the current designation "Amitābha Sūtra" is an abbreviation of the full title.
Śāriputra, in the world-system to the south, there are the Buddhas Candrasūryapradīpa, Yaśaḥprabha, and Mahārciskandha.
The Buddha Sumerudīpa, the Buddha Amitavīrya, and other Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
each in their respective lands, extend their broad and long tongues, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and speak words of truth: "You sentient beings,
you should believe in this praise of inconceivable merit, which is protected by all Buddhas."
As for the name *Jñānābhibhū* (He Who Surpasses by Renown): his fame is heard in other realms, like the intensity of a brilliant light. As for *Arciṣmān* (Flaming Shoulder):
his merit and wisdom shall manifest upon his person, like flames issuing from both shoulders.
Śāriputra, regarding the six directions mentioned in this sutra: the western world refers to beyond one hundred trillion buddha-lands from Sahā and Sukhāvatī;
the eastern direction refers to the east of Sahā, and the western direction refers to the west of Sukhāvatī. Thus, there are infinite easts and wests. Therefore—
There are Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who extensively designate the western direction and specifically name their worlds;
from this, it can be known that they do not point to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Among them is the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.
The name of this Buddha happens to be identical to an alternative name for Amitābha Buddha; these are what are known as "Buddhas of the Same Name.
Whenever a Buddha appears, there are immeasurable others who share the same name—whether appearing before him, after him, or simultaneously.
Just as a single Buddha may have many names, so too may many Buddhas share a single name. Thus, the names of each Buddha are like clouds of lamps.
The Moon in Water; Buddha of Immeasurable Marks;
Buddha of the Immeasurable Banner; Buddha of Great Radiance; Buddha of Great Brilliance; Buddha of Jewel Marks; Buddha of Pure Light.
All these Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, each within their own land, extend their broad and long tongues until they completely cover the trichiliocosm,
and speak these words of truth: "You sentient beings,
you should believe this Sutra on the Merit of Inconceivable Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas."
"Immeasurable Banner" refers to the light-marks of the Buddha’s merit and wisdom; it is as lofty and bright as a banner, and moreover, it is inexhaustible.
Śāriputra, in the world-systems of the northern direction, there are Buddhas such as Flame Shoulder, Most Victorious Sound, Irresistible, Sun-Born, and Net-Luminosity.
In worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, these and other Buddhas each, within their respective lands, emit broad and long [tongues].
His tongue-mark extends to cover the entire trichiliocosm. He speaks words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sutra on the Merit of Immeasurable Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas."

"Difficult to obstruct" means that the Buddha-nature is heroic and fierce, and cannot be suppressed or checked. "Born of the sun" means it is like the sun first rising, its radiance and flames blazing intensely.
Śāriputra, in the worlds below there are Buddhas— Sīha Buddha, Yaśas Buddha, Jyotis Buddha, Dharma Buddha,
Dharmadhvaja Buddha, and Dharmadhara Buddha— and other such Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each in their own land,
extending their broad and long tongues to completely cover the trichiliocosm and speaking words of truth: "O sentient beings..."
You should believe that this is the *Sūtra Praised for Its Inconceivable Merit and Protected by All Buddhas*.
"Siṃha" means the king among all beasts; "Tathāgata" means the king among all dharmas;
it is because of these meanings that he is so named. "Dharma" is translated here as "dharma."
Śāriputra, in the world-system above, there are the Buddhas Brahmaghoṣa,
Nakṣatrarāja, Gandhottama, Gandhaprabha, Mahārciskandha, Citraratnapuṣpavicitritaśarīra, Sālendrarāja, and Ratnakusumaguṇa.
They saw the Buddha Sarvārthadarśin, the Buddha Merukalpa, and other Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River,
each in their respective lands, extending their broad and long tongues to completely cover the trichiliocosm and speaking words of truth.
"You sentient beings, you should believe in this Sutra which extols inconceivable merit and is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
The moon is the king among the constellations, just as the Buddha is the king among all dharmas. As for 'Superior Fragrance,' it refers to the Buddha."
Fragrance is the supreme among all fragrances. As for "fragrant light," it means that the mind’s faith becomes fragrance, and through the purity of that fragrance, light is emitted.
"Adorned" (yán) means decorated. "Sāla" translates here as "firm and solid. "King of Trees" refers to a great tree.
Regarding "Virtue of Jewel Flowers": the nature of these jewel flowers is luminous, moist, and fully blossomed, such that they evoke the sensation of a fragrant aroma.
Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is this called "The Sūtra Protected by the Recollection of All Buddhas"?

Śāriputra, if there are good men or good women who hear this sūtra and accept and uphold it, as well as those who hear the names of the Buddhas—all such good men and good women shall be protected by all the Buddhas.
They all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The minds of all Buddhas are identical; they do not distinguish between self and other. Therefore, when sentient beings recite the name of a single Buddha, immeasurable Tathāgatas rejoice.

*An* means "none" (*na*). *Uttara* means "supreme" (*agra*). *Samyak* means "perfectly equal" (*samyak-samāna*). *Saṃbodhi*— [Note: The term *saṃbodhi* is left untranslated here as it is part of the compound *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which refers to supreme, perfect enlightenment.]
It is Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). Ordinary beings do not seek Perfect Enlightenment. Non-Buddhists seek Perfect Enlightenment, yet they do so incorrectly.
Arhats resemble Perfect Enlightenment, yet they are not equal to it. Only when one is equal to the supreme Buddhas above and the sentient beings below can one be said to be "equal.
Nevertheless, although Bodhisattvas are equal, they are not without supremacy. This is the Unsurpassed, Perfectly Equal, Perfect Enlightenment. Thus...
This is the Buddha. One does not regress from the path to Buddhahood because of hearing this sutra and hearing of the Buddha.
The power of this sutra is thus great. It is the same protection; it is the same mindfulness; it is the same vision of it as the perfectly interfused, single awakening.
There is no principle of retrogression. Seeing that [the Buddha] enters the wondrous through causes and conditions is the same; there is no capacity for retrogression.
If one personally retreats from the mind of nianfo, then one is inverted and contrary, and the Buddha cannot protect such a person.

○ The principal and its attendants are layered upon one another, manifesting perfectly and simultaneously, all without departing from my own single thought-moment. It is like a mirror manifesting nothing...
It is like the light of a mirror; within that light, mirror after mirror reflects one another. Alas! Why must it be the *Avataṃsaka*?
Why must it not be the *Avataṃsaka*?
Therefore, Śāriputra, you and all others should faithfully accept my words, as well as what has been spoken by all the Buddhas.
Neither believing nor accepting, all dharmas lack spiritual efficacy; yet a single phrase that enters the spirit brings joy to all Buddhas.
Why is this? All sentient beings move within the heart of the Tathāgata, and all Tathāgatas abide within the hearts of sentient beings.
It is neither moving nor abiding; it is solely the perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening.
This is all. You should believe and accept it; it is accessible to both sages and ordinary people. How should we, our kind, exert ourselves even more?
The single gateway of the Pure Land is the dojo where boundless sages and worthies gather. It is said that one suddenly awakens to one's own mind.
Those who do not require mindfulness of the Buddha to attain rebirth—how could they truly be superior to Śāriputra, whose wisdom was foremost?
Now, regarding the *Contemplation Sūtra*’s delineation of the nine grades: the upper grade is the realm of Bodhisattvas, and the middle grade is the realm of Arhats;
who would say that such sages and worthies do not seek rebirth?
Śāriputra, if there are those who have already made the vow,
or those who have already been born [in that state],
or those who are now making the vow.
If you are to be reborn in this life,
you should make a vow; if you are to be reborn in a future life, you should likewise make a vow.

For those who wish to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, that pure land of the Buddha encompasses all three [realms] within one; it is the dwelling place of the Buddhas alone, the Constantly Quiescent Light (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*).

The dwelling places of the Bodhisattvas manifested within that light are the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction (*samyaktvavipākānāvaraṇabhūmi*). As for the dwelling places of the Śrāvakas manifested therein...

This refers to the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*). The dwelling places manifested for sentient beings refer to the Land of Common Abode of Ordinary Beings and Sages (*prthagjana-ārya-sahavāsa-bhūmi*).
