When the mirror-light perfectly encompasses all, the four lands are fundamentally fused; as soon as one falls into the trap of words and thought, they become but a single land.
If a person of the highest intelligence awakens to the fact that the high is the low and the low is the high, then when the mind is empty, the environment becomes numinous.
They shall make the vow to be reborn there; there is no need for deliberation, for it will surely come to pass.
All these people shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Whether they have already been born in that land, or...
If one carries [the practice] from a previous life, one includes the phrase "having already made the vow";
if in this present life, one includes the phrase "making the vow now. This latter phrase is the most significant.
If you are to be reborn, you must utter the words of the vow; if you make the vow now, then rebirth occurs now.
With the drumstick already in hand, do you worry that the drum will not sound? Quickly face Amitābha and reverently extend your repentance.
Therefore, Śāriputra, all sons of good family and daughters of good family who possess faith should make a vow to be born in that land.
As Śākyamuni was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he left behind this single sutra without waiting for further inquiry or consultation, earnestly exhorting us with repeated instructions.

Furthermore, the Dharma within this sutra is the most concise of the concise, the easiest of the easy, the swiftest of the swift, the most secure of the secure, the most transcendent of the transcendent, and the most perfect of the perfect.
Alas! Reaching this point, his grace has reached its ultimate limit.
However, the ocean of karma contains many bubbles; birth and extinction are inherently limited. Habitual tendencies are formed over many lifetimes, yet the wondrous Dharma is heard but once.
The power of faith is like a firefly’s glow, hardly able to withstand the wind and rain; thus, among those who make vows, not even one in a hundred succeeds.
Those who practice the recollection of the Buddha fill the world, yet I do not know to what end their efforts lead.
Śāriputra, just as I now praise the inconceivable merit of all Buddhas,
so too do those Buddhas praise my own inconceivable merit, saying these words:
These words refer to the following sixty characters:
Śākyamuni Buddha was able to perform a most difficult and rare feat;

he was able, within the Sahā world-system, amidst the five turbidities of the evil age—the turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life—to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[He attained] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For the sake of all sentient beings, he preached this Dharma which is difficult for all the world to believe.
Śākyamuni: "Śākya" means "Capable One" (Nengren); "Muni" means "Silent Sage" (Jimo). These two matters—attaining Buddhahood and preaching the Dharma—are extremely difficult and rare.
It is not difficult to attain Buddhahood; what is difficult is to attain Buddhahood amidst the five turbidities. To preach [the Dharma]...
The Dharma is not difficult; what is difficult is to preach the Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe.
The "kalpa-turbidity" (kalpa-kaṣāya) is formed by the conjunction of the four turbidities. "Views" refers to delusion. "Afflictions" (kleśa) refers to the lack of mastery over body and mind.

"Sentient beings" (sattva) refers to those who grasp at the impurity of the aggregates (skandha), receiving evil names and foul appellations. "Life" (āyus) refers to the inability of form and mind to maintain one another with stability.
It has been long indeed. O, our Śākyamuni, within this defiled and evil world, manifested the body of a Tathāgata and preached this single, subtle, and exquisite Dharma.
He excavated the ordinary mind to open the aperture of the sage; he exchanged poisonous medicine for the gift of *amṛta*.
This is the grace beyond grace, the benefit among all benefits. Yet we, for our part, remain firm in worldly views...

Imprisoned by the evil roots that are difficult to uproot, one hears the teaching yet does not believe it; thus, one’s entire life passes in vain. When one emerges from this state again, one knows not when it shall be.
This may truly be called a profound abandonment of the Buddha’s grace.
Śāriputra, the following are the words spoken by Śākya himself; therefore, he again calls out the name of Śāriputra.
You should know that in this world of five turbidities, I have performed this difficult task and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
To preach this dharma so difficult to believe for the sake of all the worlds—this is truly most difficult.

As the words flow in continuous succession and circle back upon one another, with host and guest mutually reflecting, to reach this point and then further describe its own difficulty means that every character is a trace of blood, entirely bearing a lustrous and transparent quality. Alas! I and the Tathāgata share this same...
Mind! Why do you doubt your own mind instead of using the mind to recite the Buddha’s name?
Knowing that this matter ultimately returns to a single ease can resolve the Tathāgata’s twofold anxiety. The Buddha rejoices; I rejoice.
The entire shadow of the Pure Land manifests within the mind. Because this power is so exceedingly easy, people cannot believe it;
thus, it becomes a difficult teaching. Alas! How can the clumsiness of sentient beings reach such a state?

The Buddha within your own mind has already appeared, and you have already expounded the various teachings of the mind-dharma. Yet you are like one who, facing a mirror, mistakes their own head for another—madly deluded.
The four departures are all instances of losing one’s mind and failing to look back. When the exposition of the sutra reaches this point, skillful means are exhausted;

beyond this, neither mind nor Buddha appears. If one contemplates the Buddha with clear understanding and vows that penetrate the boundless, then one transcends all worlds, and both "difficult" and "easy" practices become mere conceptual play.
The pure land manifests within the mind, and the mind itself attains rebirth there.
Like a mirror within a mirror, their radiance is non-dual.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Śāriputra, the bhikṣus, and all those in the world— gods, humans, asuras, and others—
[were filled with joy].
Asura: This is translated as "Non-God. They possess the blessings of the gods but lack the virtues of the gods, and they are constantly at war with them.
If they turn their hearts toward the Buddha, the three poisons will vanish in an instant, and they shall return to the Pure Land; they will no longer be the same beings as they were before.
Hearing what the Buddha has taught, they rejoice and accept it with faith.
This joy is the soaring mind; it is the faculty for transcending the Sahā world. This acceptance with faith is the pure vow;
it is the aperture through which one reaches the Ultimate Bliss. When these faculties and apertures are clear and resonant, the perfect mind reflects in all four directions.
Having paid homage, they departed.
Above the character "departed" (qu), there is the sense of a decisive intention to go.
This is from the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Buddha-spoken Amitābha Sūtra).
These six characters should also be recited.
Regarding the *Dhāraṇī for Eradicating the Root of All Karmic Obstacles and Attaining Birth in the Pure Land*:
those who recite the Buddha’s name but fail to attain rebirth therein do so because of the obstruction of evil karma. Its root is firm and stable; its branches...
The branches are lush and dense; boundless karmic creditors and illusory shadows layer upon one another.

Were it not for the empowerment of the Buddha’s power, how could one transcend this life to be reborn in the Pure Land? *Dhāraṇī* means "total retention"; it refers to encompassing all phenomena and upholding immeasurable meanings.
In this land, it is also called a *mantra*. This is the *Wǎngshēng Zhòu* (Rebirth Mantra). Recite it three times during the ritual session.
Pervasive. Namo Amitābhāya. Tathāgatāya. Tadyathā:
Amitabhe, Amitābhe, Spharaṇe, Amitābhe, Vikaraṇate, Amitā...
*Trīṭa. Vikaraṇe. Gamine. Gagane. Citakale. Svāhā.* (Note: *ṭa* sounds like *da*; *ta* sounds like *tuo*; *ga* sounds like *jia*; *pi* sounds like *pi*; *dan* sounds like *tan*;
*ni* is pronounced with the *ru* and *li* initials; *na* is pronounced with the *nu* and *he* initials; *ci* sounds like *zhi*; *lei* sounds like *li*).
This mantra is a secret word (*mantra*); one should not seek its literal meaning. Recite it with a focused mind, and there will be marvelous responses.
The recitation of the sutra and dharanis being concluded, next the praise of the Buddha is raised:
"The body of Amitābha Buddha is golden in color; His marks and signs and radiant light are peerless.

"Amitābha Buddha" refers collectively to the three bodies: the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). "Body golden in color" specifically indicates the Reward-body.
His marks are vast while his features are exquisite; there is none equal to him, nothing with which he can be compared.
"The white tuft curls like five Mount Sumerus; his deep blue eyes are as clear as the four great oceans.
This is a forced analogy made within that which is beyond comparison. Between his two eyebrows is a white tuft with eight facets.
It is hollow within and curls to the right. Its size is equal to five Mount Sumerus. "Azure" (gān) means dark blue.
"The four great oceans" is said to indicate its vastness; all of these refer to the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body).
Within the light, there appear countless billions of manifested Buddhas, and the assembly of manifested Bodhisattvas is likewise boundless.
These manifested Buddhas vary in size; the large ones are a thousand feet tall, while the small ones are sixteen feet. Each manifested Buddha has two manifested Bodhisattvas as attendants:
Avalokiteśvara on the left and Mahāsthāmaprāpta on the right. This is what occurs for one who is ill at the time of rebirth in the Pure Land.
The Buddha seen who provides guidance and reception is precisely this transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Through the forty-eight vows, he delivers sentient beings, causing those of the nine grades (*navavidha*) to all ascend to the other shore.
"Nine grades" refers to the number of lotus tiers; within each of the superior, middling, and inferior categories, each is further divided into superior, middling, and inferior sub-categories.
Intermediate and inferior [levels of practice], thus forming nine grades. "The Other Shore" (Pāra) refers to the place where the Way is realized.
*Namo* to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One.
Non-attachment is the Great [Vow]; uprooting suffering is Compassion; bestowing happiness is Loving-kindness.
Chanting the four characters "A-mi-tuo-fo" (Amitābha Buddha) one time—taking a thousand recitations as the standard for each session—one must recite them without beginning or end.
The tail: every phrase is like a single phrase; it is naturally luminous and translucent.
When every word and every sound are linked in continuous radiance, there is no need for chanting.
Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Generally speaking, "namo" signifies the meaning of taking refuge. This bodhisattva illuminates the world with the eye of the mind and is able to perceive sounds.
When worldly people recite this bodhisattva’s name, light arises within their hearts, and they naturally perceive those sounds. One should...
At the time of contemplating Avalokiteśvara, one is neither identical to nor distinct from this Bodhisattva;

thus, one is able to obtain spiritual responses and fulfill one's aspirations, ultimately being reborn in the Western Land. [One should] chant each of the three names of the three types of Bodhisattvas three times.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
With great resolve and great power, wherever his body goes, the worlds tremble. Upon his head is a precious vase from which light radiates incessantly.
He also manifests small bodies that enter this Sahā world, specifically to take hold of those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and cause them to attain it.
They shall return to the Pure Land. This Bodhisattva, through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
He said: "Completely gather the six sense faculties; let pure mindfulness continue without interruption. Without relying on expedient means, one will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind."
Homage to the Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean Assembly.
Their number is as vast as the waters of the great ocean. Having accomplished their mental karma and long resided in Sukhāvatī, they are therefore pure.
Even with one Buddha and two Bodhisattvas, the radiance of their causal conditions is not slight; this is further augmented by this oceanic assembly.
The Bodhisattvas, each by the power of their vows and conditions, come to rescue their kinsmen.
With a single cry, the wind stirs the heart of the lotus; the body of one person is illuminated by all the radiant lights.
Next, kneel and recite the *Western Pure Land Vow* composed by Master Lianchi once.

If you are joyful at first but subsequently grow weary and lax, this cannot be called "aspiration. To speak of the Pure Land with the mouth while the heart remains attached to this Sahā world is not true resolve.
One must not call this a mere "vow. Let those who recite these words reflect upon them:
I bow my head to the Great Teacher in the West, the Land of Peace and Bliss, Who receives and guides all sentient beings.
I now make this vow: may I be reborn there. I pray only that you, in your compassion, will take me in with your grace. (叩)

I, your disciple, universally for the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, seek the unsurpassed path of Bodhi through the One Vehicle of all Buddhas;
therefore, with single-minded devotion, I shall hold in mind and recite the great name of Amitābha Buddha, endowed with ten thousand virtues, aspiring to be born in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, because my karma is heavy and my merit is light, my obstructions are deep and my wisdom is shallow...
Shallow afflictions easily flare up, while pure virtues are difficult to accomplish.
Now, before the Buddha, with uplifted diligence and prostrating the five limbs, I lay bare my single mind and offer this sincere repentance.

I and all sentient beings, since the beginningless kalpas, have been deluded regarding our inherently pure mind; we have indulged in greed, anger, and ignorance, defiling the three karmas. Immeasurable...
May all the karmic stains of offenses committed throughout the boundless reaches of space, and all the retributive karma of enmities thus incurred, be entirely extinguished.
From this day forth, I establish this profound vow: to remain far removed from unwholesome dharmas and vow never to create them again;
to diligently cultivate the Noble Path and vow never to fall back or become indolent; to vow to attain Perfect Enlightenment and vow to deliver all sentient beings.
Born [in that land], Amitābha Buddha—by the power of his compassionate vows—shall bear witness to me;
he shall take pity on me; he shall bestow his grace upon me.
May I, within my meditative contemplation and even during my dreams, behold the golden body of Amitābha Buddha and traverse the precious adornments of Amitābha Buddha’s [Pure Land].
In that land, may I receive the *amṛta* consecration from Amitābha Buddha, his radiance illuminating my body, his hand stroking my head, and his robe covering my form.

May my past karmic obstructions be naturally eliminated, my roots of goodness increase, my afflictions swiftly emptied, and ignorance suddenly shattered. May the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment become vast and expansive.
Awakening to the true realm of *sambhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, one constantly manifests the *dharmakāya*.
When the time of death approaches, one knows in advance that the moment has arrived. The body is free from all illness, suffering, and calamities;

the mind is free from all greed, attachment, and delusion. The faculties are joyful and serene, right mindfulness is clear and distinct, and one casts off the physical report with composure and tranquility.
As if entering meditative concentration, Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of holy sages,
emit light to welcome and guide them, extending their hands to lead them forth. Multi-storied pavilions, banners, and streamers, along with extraordinary fragrances and celestial music—
the sacred realms of the West— are manifested before one's eyes, enabling all sentient beings who see or hear this to [attain liberation].
They rejoiced with great joy and, moved by deep inspiration, gave rise to the bodhicitta.

At that time, riding upon a vajra-throne and following behind the Buddha, in the mere blink of an eye, I was born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, within a lotus flower of supreme excellence inside a pond of the seven treasures.
Upon the opening of the flower, I beheld the Buddha and saw all the bodhisattvas, and heard the sublime Dharma.

Upon hearing [the sound], they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). In a mere instant, they served all Buddhas and personally received their predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

Having received these predictions, they fully accomplished the three bodies (*trikāya*), the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates, and all merits. Thereafter...
Without departing from the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), he returns to enter the Sahā world; manifesting countless bodies, he pervades the lands of the ten directions.
By means of inconceivable and sovereign spiritual powers, and through various skillful means, he delivers and liberates sentient beings.
May all be led to leave behind defilement, regain a pure mind, be born together in the Western Land, and enter the stage of non-retrogression.
Such are my great vows: as long as worlds are inexhaustible, sentient beings are inexhaustible, and karma and afflictions are entirely inexhaustible, may my vows be inexhaustible.
May I now pay homage to the Buddha, make these vows, and practice.
Holding these merits, I dedicate them to all sentient beings. May the four debts of gratitude be fully repaid; may those in the three realms of existence be equally sustained.
May all beings throughout the Dharma-realm together realize the Perfect Wisdom. [叩] (Kou).

Regarding the four debts of gratitude: for those in the household, they are heaven and earth, the sovereign, one's parents, and the teacher; for those who have left the household, they are one's parents, the teachers and the Sangha, the king, and the donors.
Regarding the three realms of existence: these are the three worlds. Regarding the sentient beings of the dharma-realm: [they are all as described above].
It refers to all sentient beings throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions. Because the mind can transport all dharmas, it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*).
With the Buddha as its ultimate goal, and not falling into duality or plurality, it is called the "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*).

"Developing and purifying" means to cast oneself in sincere devotion, surrendering one's own mind to the Buddha. "Repentance" means severing the continuity of the deluded mind.
Regarding the mention of "myself and all sentient beings," those who seek birth in the Pure Land must possess a vast and expansive mind;
only by contemplating all as a single essence can they accord with the vows of the Buddha. Thus, when one person repents, it is the repentance of all sentient beings.
This is repentance. ○ All karmic actions are not called "fixed. If one repents them, they vanish; if one leaves them as they are, they persist.
One must believe that they can be extinguished—repenting once, they are extinguished. Why is this? Because the power of the mind is the strongest. ○ There are three kinds of grievances:
the grievance of killing, the grievance of stealing, and the grievance of sexual misconduct. Killing and stealing are termed "grievances of anger"; sexual misconduct is termed...
Delight in enemies. All sentient beings take their enemies for kin. If the merit of one’s mindfulness of the Buddha is profound, one will perceive all enemies and kin as being like light or shadows;
thus, rebirth in the Pure Land will be free from entanglements. Meditative contemplation and the recitation of the name are originally two distinct methods.
However, if one realizes the meaning of the scriptures, one should imagine that the sound of one’s own recitation of the Buddha’s name enters directly into the Western Paradise.
Amidst the wind-swept trees, the spiritual birds, the flowing water, the radiant light, the precious pavilions, and the celestial music merge into a single, seamless whole;
this is precisely the non-duality of visualization and the recitation of the name. This is called the Western Dhyāna, and it is also called the Dhyāna of Sound.
As for the suffering of illness, it is the disharmony of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). As for calamities and misfortunes, they include water, fire, weapons, and toxic drugs.

"Kindred" (*lei*) refers to those who are greedily attached; they make vows and seek physicians, yet harbor resentment for eating meat. "Deluded" (*mei-huo*) refers to those who doubt that their offenses are many and their merits few, and thus fear that the Buddha will not come to welcome them.
"Retribution" (*bao*) refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). "Shedding retribution" means at the moment of passing away, one abandons this retribution body and the spirit proceeds alone.
As for "patience with the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), all phenomena are fundamentally non-arising from the very beginning.
Birth is non-extinguishing. Since one has become a sentient being, there are inverted and deluded views; now, by means of wisdom, one thoroughly realizes this, and thus it is called "attainment.
Once this patience (*kṣānti*) is attained, the Great Function is finally accomplished. The Three Bodies (*trikāya*) are the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body.
The Four Wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) arise when the delusions of the eight consciousnesses return to their source and realize the Truth, transforming consciousness into wisdom. Its...
There are four categories. Regarding the eight consciousnesses: the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body constitute the first five consciousnesses; the mind (*manas*) is the sixth consciousness;

the subtle mind that does not perceive external objects is called the seventh consciousness; and the fundamental capacity of the mind that contains and stores seeds is called the eighth consciousness.
For one who cultivates the path, these first five consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
The transformation of the sixth consciousness results in the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; the transformation of the seventh consciousness results in the Wisdom of Equality;
and the transformation of the eighth consciousness results in the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. The five eyes are: the flesh eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.

The six supernormal powers are: the power of the divine ear, the power of the divine eye, the power of psychic mobility, the power of knowing others' minds, the power of recollecting past lives, and the power of the destruction of outflows.
This is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā). Regarding the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika-bhūmi), there are three meanings:

first, non-retrogression in status, meaning one never again regresses to the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) or a follower of the two vehicles (śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha); second, non-retrogression in practice, meaning one never loses the karmic activities of the path being cultivated;
third, non-retrogression in mindfulness, meaning the thought of bodhicitta never momentarily regresses or turns back. Furthermore, it is said: "Even if one’s grade is the lowest of the low..."
Though one may be confined within the city of doubt, by eternally severing the causes for the three miserable realms, this is also called "non-retrogression.
○ Regarding the fourth point—that the karmic afflictions of birth within the realms are not yet exhausted—my great vow likewise shall never be exhausted.
By mobilizing this inexhaustible power of the vow to deliver these inexhaustible sentient beings, one truly manifests the light of the immeasurable mind, which is able to equal that of Amitābha.

This is in harmony. ○ *Zhongzhi* (All-encompassing Wisdom) is the Buddha-wisdom; it refers to the ability to penetrate both the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and the infinite characteristics. ○ Someone asked:

To cling to the principle of life with a deadened attachment is called a fool. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "One enters meditative absorption within the wind."
One enters meditative concentration within the sounds [of chanting]. An ancient master said: "Walking is Chan; sitting is also Chan.

This means that when one practices the recitation of the name while walking, the numinous spirit is already in meditative concentration. Someone asked: "Those who practice the visualization of the West see the Buddha.
Can those who practice the recitation of the name see the Buddha during their recitation? He replied: "Visualizing the Buddha employs the mind's eye; this is a form within the mind."

"Hold the name and listen with the mind; this is the sound within the mind. Yet when the mind contemplates the Buddha’s form, and the Buddha appears and preaches the Dharma, there is a wondrous sound.
When the mind listens to the Buddha’s voice, the spirit becomes concentrated and auspicious signs appear, and there is a wondrous form."
The six sense objects and the myriad dharmas revolve solely within the mind. My son, simply listen with your spirit to the sound of your own recitation of the Buddha’s name.
After a long, long time, when at one moment the drums have fallen silent and the bells have subsided, you shall meet the Tathāgata face to face.
